notes: Tier 2 narrative-craft rubric. Unlike Tier 1 (deterministic pattern matching, no model call), these items are genuinely judgment calls — the MCP tools here don't grade text themselves. get_prose_craft_rubric hands the calling agent one named rubric item's definition; the agent applies it using its own judgment and reports a verdict back through grade_prose_craft, which structures that verdict into a Finding. This keeps CanvasLoop free and self-hostable (no model API call embedded in the server) and matches the TRD's own framing: 'one named rubric item checked at a time, definition supplied in-context — not an open does-this-sound-natural prompt.'

rubric.name: Self-justifying / over-explaining
rubric.definition: The line explains or justifies its own word choice, design decision, or boundary instead of simply stating the fact — as if pre-answering a question the reader never asked, or narrating the writer's reasoning process instead of just the conclusion. A frequent tell: stating not just what something IS, but also, at length, everything it ISN'T.
rubric.howToCheck: Read the line and ask: does it do more than state what's true? Does it also explain WHY it's phrased that way, defend against a possible misreading, or exhaustively rule out alternatives nobody proposed? If you cut the justification/caveat clause, does the line still say everything the reader actually needs? If yes, the justification is padding — flag it.

bad: Named for coffee on purpose — there is no way to write "a cup of coffee" that could pass for an in-game reward.
Nothing that helps you. No coin, no heroes, no gear, no shortcuts, no second chances — there is nowhere in this game to put money down and come out ahead of where you were.
good: Buy someone a coffee. It doesn't do anything in the game.
This is a tip jar. It's not a shop.

rubric.fixHint: Cut the justification clause. State the fact once, plainly, and trust the reader not to need the reasoning spelled out.
rubric.note: Found through direct dogfooding on a real project's IAP/settings screen, not derived from external craft literature — the source here is the failure mode itself, observed firsthand.

source.name: Direct dogfooding (Kurogane Saga 'Support the game' screen)

rubric.name: On-the-nose dialogue
rubric.definition: A character states their own emotion, intent, or thought directly instead of it coming through indirectly — tone, subtext, a non-answer, an action, a deflection. The audience is told the feeling rather than shown it.
rubric.howToCheck: Does the line name the emotion or intent as a fact about the speaker ("I'm angry," "I don't trust you") rather than letting it show through word choice, what's left unsaid, or how the character acts? Would a real person in this moment actually say the plain version out loud, or would they more likely deflect, joke, go quiet, or answer a different question?

bad: I'm angry because you betrayed me.
good: You always did know how to make an entrance.

rubric.fixHint: Cut the direct statement of feeling/intent. Let it show through tone, a deflection, an action, or a non-answer instead.

source.name: No Film School: What is 'On the Nose' Dialogue?

rubric.name: Exposition dump / "As You Know, Bob"
rubric.definition: A character explains something to another character that both of them would already know, purely so the reader/player learns it — the Turkey City Lexicon's named example of this exact failure, also called 'maid and butler dialogue.'
rubric.howToCheck: Would the character receiving this line plausibly already know what's being said to them? If a real conversation between these two people would never include this explanation — because they'd both already have this information — it's an exposition dump written for the audience's benefit, not the character's.

bad: As you know, the kingdom has been at war with the northern clans for a decade.
You remember how the guild only accepts bounties over rank three, right?
good: Another northern-clan bounty. Ten years and they still haven't learned.

rubric.fixHint: Cut the explanation from the dialogue. If the player genuinely needs the information, move it to something that has a reason to state it plainly — an item description, a journal entry, an environmental detail — rather than a character saying it aloud.
